REJB 2003-39500 - Texte
intégral

CITATION: B. (S.-B.) v. M. (J.-Be.)

Cour
supérieure

CANADA

PROVINCE DE QUÉBEC

DISTRICT DE  de Montréal

NO : 500-05-009878-891

DATE :  2003-03-28

EN PRÉSENCE DE :

Israël S. Mass
, J.C.S.

B. (S.-B.)

Plaintiff

v.

M. (J.-Be.)

Defendant

Israel S. Mass, j.s.c.:-

1
Alleging a breach of an
obligation assumed in a Consent to Corollary Relief confirmed by the Court by
way of a Decree Nisi, Plaintiff seeks damages from Defendant in the amount of
$1,350,000.00. Defendant, invoking questions of law and fact, contests
Plaintiff's right to seek any such damages or, alternatively, the amount of any
award.

PUBLICITY BAN

2
By judgment of March 16
th
, 2000, the Court imposed a publicity
ban in this matter under the following terms:

RULING FOR THE
MEDIAS

In view of some of
the sensitive issues which have come before the Court to this moment in this
trial, and may continue to come before the Court in this trial, any reports in
the media concerning any testimony adduced shall in no way identify either of
the parties or any of the witnesses, nor shall the contents and description of
any of the exhibits be reproduced or identified.

3
Inasmuch as
the present action derives originally from a family matter and involves
evidence of a highly personal nature, such as psychological and medical
reports, children's testimony, etc. and in virtue of Article 815.4 C.P.C., the
court is of the opinion that the aforesaid publicity ban should continue to
remain in force from the present date without any limitation of time and with
the express hope that such ban will be respected outside the Court's
territorial jurisdiction.

THE RELEVENT FACTS

4
The parties,
both previously divorced, were married on July 27, 1969. They ceased
cohabitation in 1979. A Decree Nisi of Divorce was granted to them on October
23, 1980. It ordered the parties to comply with the Consent to Corollary Relief
(the Consent) signed by them and their respective attorneys on October 23, 1980
(P –2). A Decree Absolute of Divorce under the then existing procedures
was granted on February 9, 1981 (P-1).

5
There were
two children issue of marriage, namely Allison born on November 11, 1976 and
E... A... born on [...], 1978.

6
Paragraph
12 of the Consent reads as follows:

The parties appear
before the Rabbinical authorities in the City and District of Montreal for the
purpose of obtaining the traditional religious Get, immediately upon a Decree
Nisi of Divorce being granted.

7
During the
parties' cohabitation, and unbeknownst to Defendant, Plaintiff was involved in
an extra-marital affair which led to her becoming pregnant and undergoing an
abortion on June 19, 1979.

8
Shortly
after the divorce, Plaintiff, either personally or through various Rabbis,
called upon Defendant to present himself before the Rabbinical authorities as
set out in the said paragraph 12.

9
Defendant
consistently refused to do so on the grounds that Plaintiff's behaviour towards
him since the Divorce constituted harassment and an attempt by her to alienate
him from his children.

10
Plaintiff
instituted the present action on July 24, 1989 seeking damages in the amount of
$500,000.00 as follows

a)

for having been restrained from going on
with her life since the Decree Nisi of Divorce

$

200
000.00

b)

for having been restrained to remarry
according to the Jewish faith

200
000.00

c)

for having been restricted of having
children

100
000.00

$

500 000.00

11
By letter
addressed to Defendant on November 12, 1990 and received by him on November 20,
1990 (P-3), Plaintiff formally put Defendant in default to comply with the
obligation assumed by him in the said paragraph 12.

12
Defendant
could not justify in law his failure to consent to the Get when and as
requested of him. This refusal was conceived by him as a means of punishing
Plaintiff for allegedly alienating him from his two daughters and the
multiplicity of Plaintiff's demands for money. In short, he chose this method
as a form of punishment or constraint.

13

Ultimately, on December 5, 1995, following an Order of the Court issued under

Article 21.1(3)
of the
Divorce Act
, a Certificate of Divorce was issued by the
Rabbinical Court of Montreal with Defendant's consent and participation (P-5)
(the Get).

14

Thereafter, Plaintiff amended her action to increase the mount of the damages
claimed to $1,350,000.00 as follows:

a)

for having been restrained from going on
with her life since the Decree Nisi of Divorce

$

200
000.00

b)

for having been restrained to remarry
according to the Jewish faith

200
000.00

c)

for having been restricted of having
children

200
000.00

d)

for the loss of consortium

750
000.00

$ 1 350
000,00

15
During the
period between the pronouncement of the Divorce and the Get, Plaintiff neither
remarried nor bore any children. However, she did date and have sexual
relationships with several men, none of whom proposed marriage to her.

16
During the
trial, the Court affirmed that any award of damages would be restricted to the
15 years period between the granting of the Decree Nisi on October 23, 1980 and
the Get on December 5, 1995.

THE ISSUES

1) Is Plaintiff's
claim justiciable before a civil Court?

2) If so, was there
a breach of contract by Defendant justifying an award in damages?

3) The Damages

1)

Justiciability of the claim before a
civil Court

17
May
Plaintiff's claim for damages arising from Defendant's (her ex-husband) failure
to give her a Get be decided by a civil court or must the issue remain before
the Rabbinical authorities?

18
Several
questions must be considered:

a) Does paragraph
12 of the Consent create a civil obligation or does the obligation remain in
the religious sphere?

b) What is the
difference between a court ordering a Get and ordering damages based on an
agreement made under the auspices of a civil court with respect to the
potential for infringement on the religious domain?

c) What is the
balance between religious freedom and civil responsibility that must be made,
while maintaining the separation of the Rabbinical and civil justice systems?

d) Is there a
causal link between the failure to grant the Get and the damages claimed by the
Plaintiff?

a)

The Civil Obligation

19
Defendant
claims that he had a religious obligation, not a civil one, and thus this
dispute cannot be adjudicated before a civil court. However, once the Defendant
signed a civil contract, agreeing to appear immediately before Rabbinical
authorities, this obligation moved into the realm of the civil courts, and the
religious obligation became embodied in a secular agreement. Consequently, the
Defendant had a clear and unequivocal civil law obligation to appear
“immediately” before the Rabbinical authorities. He did not appear,
however, for 15 years. Once there is a civil contract, even if its object
relates to religious obligations, it is justiciable and within the jurisdiction
of the civil court.

20

Art. 1412

of the
Civil Code of Quebec

states that the “object of the
contract is the juridical operation envisaged by the parties at the time of its
formation.” There must be an object of the contract for it to be valid.
In this case, the object of paragraph 12 of the Consent is the immediate
appearance before Rabbinical authorities «for the purposes of obtaining
the traditional religious Get…». In Quebec, the object of a
contract can be anything that is not contrary to public order (
Article 1425

C.c.Q). Since in this case there are no public order issues, the contract is
valid. Simply put, a valid civil obligation with religious undertones was
created. Since Defendant breached this obligation, Plaintiff is entitled to
seek damages before a civil court.

21
In Frame
v. Smith
1987 CanLII 74 (SCC)
, [1987] 2 S.C.R. 99 , the issue is whether a statute relied on to give
a divorce settlement can be relied on to create a cause of action. This cause
of action was denied by the court which found that the relevant statute did not
provide for damages. Defendant cites this case in an attempt to create an
analogy to the present case and to
s. 21.1
of the
Divorce Act
, which speaks to
obligations of the spouses in religious divorces, and which also does not
mention an action in damages. Defendant tries to interpret this strictly,
stating that the legislators chose to make this omission, and thus there cannot
be a cause for damages on this ground. While this may be true, Plaintiff is not
relying on
s. 21.1
as the basis of her claim. She does not need to, as she has
a contract to rely on, and does not need to try to find another cause of
action. Consequently, the analogy made by the defendant to Frame v. Smith is
not applicable in this case.

22
In
Morris
v. Morris
(1974)
1973 CanLII 1200 (MB CA)
,
42 DLR (3d) 550 (Man. C.A.)
the majority held that a civil
court cannot enforce a “Ketubah” or Jewish marriage contract to
compel a spouse to appear before a Rabbinical Court for the purpose of giving a
Get. A clear reason behind this holding was that there was no civil contract,
and the Court did not want to extend the process of the civil court to
interfere with proceedings of a religious tribunal. The case at bar can be
distinguish from
Morris v. Morris
because in this case it is not
necessary to rely on a Jewish document. An enforceable civil agreement exists.

b)

Assessing Damages Does Not Infringe on the
Religious Domain

23
Plaintiff
is not asking the civil court to order a Get. In fact, a Get was already
granted. What is being asked for in this case are damages. This substantially
changes the situation that must be addressed by the Court. While a civil court
cannot order a Get, it is beyond the scope of the Beth Din to order damages,
and a civil court is consequently not infringing on this jurisdiction..

24
In
Droit
de la famille – 2296
[1995] R.D.F. 728
, it was found that it was
meaningless to consent to a Get during a civil divorce, because no agreement,
civil or otherwise, can religiously bind a Jewish spouse to give or receive a
Get. Further, if a spouse agreed to grant a Get under court order, this would
most likely be invalid before Rabbinical authorities, because it would probably
be considered coercive and thus the consent would be invalid. However, in the
present matter, we are clearly not involved in a case in which Plaintiff is
asking the court to grant a Get and infringing on the authorities of a
religious court. Rather, Plaintiff is seeking damages stemming from the Consent
which was confirmed by the Court. In assessing and potentially granting
damages, the Court does not have to order the Rabbinical authorities to do
anything or compel either party to act on a religious obligation. Consequently,
there is no chance of making an order it cannot enforce, which courts are
clearly reluctant to do, as evidence by the reluctance in
Morris v. Morris

to not enforcing the «Ketubah» obligation to get a Jewish divorce
where necessary. In the case at bar, enforceability is not a consideration
– the Court is asked to award damages due to the breach of a civil
contract, not to enforce performance of a contract in a setting that is beyond
its jurisdiction. As Guy J. for the majority stated in
Morris v. Morris

: (op.cit.)

Courts should not
ever give judgments that cannot be enforced. As long ago as the case of Lumley
v. Wagner
(1852), I De G.M. & G. 604, 42 E.R. 687
, it was clearly stated
that no Court would order a singer to sing. Orders for specific performance of
personal services cannot be enforced. It is true, in the instant case, that Mr.
Morris could be fined or imprisoned for contempt if he failed to appear before the
rabbinical court. That would not accomplish the performance of the so-called
contract. That would simply be a matter of a superior Court in Canada demeaning
both itself and the administration of justice by delivering with great
solemnity a judgment that nobody can enforce.

25
In the
present case specific performance of the contract is not being asked for by
Plaintiff. In fact, the Get has already been given. The issue is the assessment
of damages due to Defendant's long delay in granting the Get, contrary to the
clause in the Consent. This raises no issues of enforcement of a religious
obligation. Further, while it may be true that religious authorities would not
recognize a civil agreement compelling a Jewish spouse to appear before it,
civil authorities do recognize and uphold civil contracts.

26
Defendant
criticizes Plaintiff for having instigated a civil suit in damages, implying
that she did not in fact truly care about the Get but simply wanted money. This
claim is unfounded for two reasons. First, Plaintiff could not have instituted
a civil action to force a Get, as explained above. Second, within the
limitations of the procedure under Jewish law, Plaintiff did everything that
was in her power to instigate the Get, including phone calls and letters
requesting the Get from Plaintiff, having representatives of the Jewish
community and her family call the defendant on her behalf, a formal mise en
demeure and the institution of legal proceedings.

27
All three
Rabbis who testified agreed that by the Consent, Defendant
freely
gave
his consent to appear before the Rabbinical authorities for the purposes of
obtaining the Get (Exhibit C-1). This consent was never withdrawn before the
Beth Din, and therefore remains in effect. Consequently, under Jewish law
according to the Rabbis who testified, the Get in question was an uncontested
Get as opposed to a contested or litigated Get. This distinction is relevant in
that in an uncontested Get the obligations of the male spouse to initiate
proceedings for the Get is absolute, thus no burden can be placed on Plaintiff
for failing to initiate the process, although evidence does show that she was
proactive. Defendant attempts to argue that certain procedures of community
pressure should have been initiated under Jewish law by Plaintiff had she truly
wanted to obtain the Get. While these procedures are available for contested
Gets, they are not used in uncontested Gets, as in the present matter. In
addition, the process of social pressure appears to be used rarely if ever, in
the Montreal Orthodox Jewish community. Furthermore, Defendant did eventually
give the Get of his free consent, clearly demonstrating that the Get was
uncontested, and thus making moot this discussion concerning contested or
uncontested Gets.

(emphasis added)

c)

Separation of Religious and Secular Justice
Systems is Maintained

28
While the
court reserves to the Rabbinical authorities the issue of a Jewish divorce,
assessing damages based on the breach of a civil law obligation, albeit one
with religious undertones, must remain in the domain of the civil court.

29
In order
to make an assessment of damages in this matter, the court does not have to
examine Jewish law at length, which it is obviously not equiped to do, and is
consequently not infringing of the domain of the religious authorities. In
Levitts
Kosher Foods Inc. v. Rabbi Mordechai Levin
, [99-CV-163952-CM] the Ontario
Superior Court of Justice found that the case was not justiciable because it
raised profoundly Jewish principles that the court was not qualified to decide.
This is not the same in the present case. While in
Levitts
in paragraph
33, the Court found that in order to assert its claim, Plaintiff had to:

call into question
the supervisory authority of the rabbis, their interpretation of the laws of
kashrut,

their views as to the trustworthiness of non-observant Jews, and the
standards which they, as a matter of conscience, believe are necessary to
fulfill their obligations. These issues are profoundly religious.

30
Accordingly,
it is possible to assess damages based on civil law principles by assessing the
facts of the case, which include an understanding of the religious context, but
do not infringe on religious principles. The obligation to appear immediately
before religious authorities does not put into question what would take place
once this was done. What is clear, is that under civil law, Defendant failed to
fulfill this contractual obligation, leading to consequences for Plaintiff in
her community. Consequently, in contrast to the
Levitts
case, this case
is justiciable. The pith and essence of what is being asked for in this case is
not religious. Again, a Get is not being asked for, rather the case is an
assessment of damages stemming from a factual situation which involves Jewish
parties and Jewish institutions – but principles of Jewish law do not
have to be examined in depth.

31
Defendant
attempts to argue that there is only a religious obligation to give a Get, with
its own procedures and repercussions under Jewish law and in the Jewish
community. He argues that a secular obligation is precluded from existing, in
spite of the fact that there is a civil contract that is enforceable before a
civil court, due to the fact that freedom of religion cannot be infringed upon
by the courts.

32
Freedom of
religion is not being infringed upon by hearing this case before a civil court.
Especially considering that Defendant has already granted the Get, and he is
not being forced or even encouraged by the courts to fulfill a religious
obligation. What the court is considering, is the delay in granting the Get,
based on a civil law agreement to act “immediately” based on free
consent from both parties. This is fundamentally different from interfering in
the role of the Rabbinical court, since the latter could not award damages in a
case such as this.

d)

Causal Link Between Breach of Contract and
Damages

33
In the
present case, the three Rabbis who testified all acknowledge that the Get was
uncontested. Therefore, when Defendant did finally appear before the Rabbinical
authorities, a Get was granted without further problems. While paragraph 12 of
the clause of the Consent to Corollary Relief stated only that Defendant
“appear” before the rabbinical authorities, it is clear that this
appearance, when it finally occurred, led to a Get. Consequently, the breach of
the civil law obligation to appear is the cause of the damages claimed by
Plaintiff. While the appearance may not have led inexorably to a Get, in this
case, it clearly did. The balance of probabilities in this case and especially,
the evidence of Rabbi Kramer, leads the Court to believe that had Defendant
sought the Get immediately when called upon to do so, it would then have been
granted by the religious authorities.

34
Defendant
attempts to argue that Plaintiff did not in fact really care about the Get, and
only wants his money. He tries to substantiate this by claiming that his
ex-wife could have appeared before the Beth Din herself to initiate the Get. It
has been shown by the testimonies of the Rabbis that, while such a procedure
may have been available to her in places like New York, it was not available to
her in Montreal. Further, while the option of an annulment of the marriage
before the Beth Din was presented by Defendant, this is not a practice
recognized by many Orthodox Rabbis, an important consideration for Plaintiff
who describes herself of the Orthodox Jewish community. She could not have
remarried within her stated community if she had a mere annulment and not a
Get. Further, an annulment was not the object of the civil law contract in the
Consent.

35
The
failure of Defendant to grant the Get for 15 years had direct consequences on
the life of Plaintiff. It deprived her of the opportunity to marry within her
community during this period.

36
Finally,
while based on the evidence, Plaintiff had no potential marriage partner, and
her moral standing has been put into question due to alleged promiscuity and
unstable relationships with her children, the issue in the present case is not
based on her morality, but the breach of a civil obligation and the potential
consequences on Plaintiff.

37
The Court
is therefore of the opinion that this present matter raises judicial issues
within its competence.

(2)

The breach of contract

38
Logically,
as appears from the Court's reasoning above, Defendant's failure to respect his
obligation under paragraph 12 of the Consent, although duly called upon to do
so, constitutes a breach of contract, subject to an award of damages.

(3)

The Damages

39
In her
Declaration of July 24, 1989, Plaintiff originally sought damages totalling
$500,000.00. She acknowledged however, that on the advice of her then attorney
and other counsellors, her intent at the time of institution of her proceedings
was not to seek damages but rather to provoke Defendant into giving her a Get.

40
It was
only after Defendant had consented to the Get, that Plaintiff amended her
Declaration to then seek damages totalling $1,350,000.00

41
Neither
party could provide the Court with any precedent or guide line for the
calculation of the quantum of damages to be awarded to Plaintiff. Rather, this
assessment was left to the entire discretion of the Court. (Ter-Neuzen c. Korn,

1995 CanLII 72 (SCC)
, [1995] 3 R.C.S. 674 )

42
It is
important to recall that the Court previously determined that «damages
would be restricted to the 15 year period between the granting of the Decree
Nisi on October 23, 1980 and the Get on December 4, 1995»

43
The Court
will examine, in term, each head of Plaintiff's claim for damages:

a)

For having been restrained from going on
with her life since the Decree Nisi of Divorce - $200,000.00

44
From the
evidence brought before the Court, Plaintiff's enjoyment of life was in no way
diminished by her failure to obtain her Get. Indeed, she testified that during
the relevant period, she had many male lovers, many friends, an active social
life and engaged in various business activities. While the various medical
records produced show that she was going through some emotional turmoil during
the relevant period, such turmoil was to a large part due to her self
questioning, her seeking to satisfy her sexual appetites and needs, and her
role in society generally.

45
There can
therefore be no award of damages under this head.

b)

For having been restrained to remarry
according to the Jewish faith. $200,000.00

46
While
there is no evidence that any suitor broke off his relationship with Plaintiff
because of her inability to marry him before a Rabbi of the Orthodox Community
– indeed there is no evidence of any offer to marry at all –
Plaintiff was nevertheless entitled to exercise her freedom of religious choice
as she alone determined it. It is not for Defendant to impose on her a degree
of «religiosity», to say that she could have remarried in the
Reform Synagogue or sought an annulment etc.

47
Matters of
religious conscience must be left to the adult parties invoking them and not be
imposed by others Plaintiff has satisfied the Court that despite her many deviations
from the doctrines and precepts of the Orthodox Jewish Community – her
abortion, extra-marital affairs, use of contraceptives, etc. – Plaintiff
was and remained a member of the Orthodox branch of the Jewish community, that
she therefore had the right to remarry before a rabbi of that community and to
do so, would have needed a Get from a Beth Din recognised by such community.

48
At the
time of the granting of her divorce, Plaintiff was only 31 years old. She was
46 when the Get was finally granted.

49
In its
discretion, the Court will award damages to Plaintiff under this head on the
basis of $2,500.00 for each of the 15 years during which Defendant refused to
consent to the Get, a total of $37,500.00

c)

For having been restricted of having children
- $200,000.00

50
The Court
presumes that any reference by Plaintiff to having children would necessarily
mean «legitimate» ones under the precept of the Orthodox Jewish
community to which she belonged

51
Since
Plaintiff failed to adduce any evidence that any relationship which could have
led to marriage had foundered on her not having a Get, she was not prevented
from having such a child with such a partner.

52
However,
since she was generally unable to have such a legitimate child and she alleges
that this affected her choice of male companions and lovers, the Court awards
her a nominal sum of $10,000.00 under this head.

d)

For the loss of consortium - $750,000.00.

53
As
previously stated, Plaintiff did not refuse any offer of marriage, and that, in
fact, one of her long term companions was a Christian or at the very least a
non-believing Jew who, in either case, would not have been affected by her not
having a Get. Moreover, Defendant testified that had Plaintiff sought a Get
from him because she had an offer of marriage, he would have immediately
consented to its granting. The Court has no reason to doubt him on this point.

54

Accordingly, no award or damages can be made under this head.

COMMENT

55
In
calculating Plaintiff's damages, none of which relate to tangible elements, the
Court had to consider and assess the subjective effect on her which resulted
from Defendant's breach of his contractual obligation, including the social
stigma of being classified as an «agunah» or «chained
women». As a result, the Court's assessment in the present case should
not be deemed to set a jurisprudential benchmark for the future.

COSTS AND INTEREST

56
Plaintiff
acknowledged that her original proceedings were destined not to seek the
damages claimed, but rather to provoke Defendant into consenting to the Get.

57
Her claim
for damages only became a real issue after the granting of the Get at which
point she produced her Amended Declaration.

58

Accordingly, interest on the damages awarded to Plaintiff as well as the
additional indemnity provided for under article 1078.1 C.C. will only commence
on the date of service of the Amended Declaration.

FOR THESE REASONS, THE COURT:

59

GRANTS

the action in part.

60

ORDERS
a
publication ban with respect to the names of the parties and their two
children.

61

RECOMMENDS

that the publication ban be respected beyond the jurisdiction of this
Court.

62

CONDEMNS

Defendant to pay to Plaintiff the sum of $47,500.00 with interest and the
additional indemnity provided under article 1078.1 C.C. from the date of
service of the Amended Declaration.

63

THE
WHOLE
with costs.

Israel S.
Mass, j.s.c.

Me Allan Stein, for Plaintiff

Me Anne France Goldwater, for Defendant
